as_told: In his Berlin speech of 26 June 1963, John F. Kennedy said "Ich bin ein Berliner". Because he added the article "ein", the sentence supposedly meant "I am a jelly doughnut", since a Berliner is a kind of doughnut. The crowd is said to have laughed at the mistake.
lesson: Kennedy's German was wrong: to Germans, and to Berliners in particular, "Ich bin ein Berliner" meant "I am a jelly doughnut", so check foreign phrases with native speakers.
what_happened: Kennedy said "Ich bin ein Berliner" twice in his speech at the Rudolph Wilde Platz on 26 June 1963. The published transcript shows that after the first use he joked "I appreciate my interpreter translating my German!"; it does not mark any laughter about a doughnut. The earliest telling of the doughnut story I found is in Len Deighton's spy novel Berlin Game (1983), spoken by the narrator Bernard Samson, who adds that Berlin cartoonists drew talking doughnuts the next day. A New York Times review of the novel (12 December 1983) then repeated it as fact. In Berlin itself the pastry is called Pfannkuchen, not Berliner.
false_part: The sentence did not mean "I am a jelly doughnut" to the Berlin crowd, and the earliest telling of the joke I found is a 1983 novel, not a 1963 record.

lesson_verdict.why: The Atlas zur deutschen Alltagssprache, a survey of everyday German usage, records that in Berlin and almost all of eastern Germany the pastry is called simply Pfannkuchen; Berliner is the name in the rest of western Germany and Switzerland. So a Berlin crowd would not have heard the sentence as a reference to a pastry.

confidence_note: The Deighton quote comes from a search snippet of the 1983 edition, so it is short. I did not hear the speech audio; the claim that the crowd laughed is judged from the transcript alone. Leads (Duden, Eichhoff 1993) say the grammar of the sentence was correct; I did not save a grammar source, so the entry does not rely on that point. The lesson verdict rests on the Atlas record of what Berliners call the pastry.
